captions.text: At dawn, every thread of a spider web holds up the others.
In a Florida spring, a manatee drifts toward the water plants it eats.
Sun, plants, water, fish, birds, gators. Out here, they're all tied together.
When the rain stops, the marsh begins to dry.
Fish crowd into the last pools, and the birds follow.
People can cut a thread, or help tie it back.
How are all the parts of nature, weather, plants, animals, and people, connected to each other?

words: All the living and nonliving things in a place, and the ways they affect each other.
When living things depend on each other to survive. What happens to one affects the others.
A trait that helps a living thing survive in its environment, like webbed feet for swimming.
The usual weather of a place over many years: the long-term pattern, not just one day.
A diagram that shows how energy moves through an ecosystem as living things eat other living things.
The ways people change the natural world. It can be harmful (pollution, habitat loss) or helpful (conservation).

parts.title: Every Living Thing Has Neighbors
parts.html:
Remember the mystery specimen? It's an owl pellet: the fur, bones, and beetle shells an owl couldn't digest. One small lump holds pieces of a food web.

Think about a Florida wetland. Fish eat tiny water plants. A heron eats the fish. An alligator may eat the heron. If the pond dries up, the fish disappear, and so does the heron. That's interdependence. Scientists call the whole connected community, living and nonliving, an ecosystem.

parts.title: Weather Writes the Rules
parts.html: Climate decides which plants can grow in a place, and plants decide which animals can live there. Florida's wet summers flood the sawgrass, and the water brings food and shelter for many birds. In the Everglades, rain sets the water level, and so do canals that people built.

parts.title: Traits, Change, and Human Hands
parts.html: Living things have adaptations that fit their home. A spoonbill sweeps its flat bill through shallow water to catch small fish. Mangrove roots hold tight in soft, flooded mud. But places can change faster than living things can adapt. People drain wetlands and cut forests. People can also choose to protect places, like Everglades National Park.

wow.title: The Gator's Water Hole
wow.alt: An old black-and-white photo of a gator hole: a small, dark pool surrounded by tall plants
wow.caption: A gator hole in Florida, photographed about 1910
wow.html:
Alligators use their snouts, feet, and tails to clear mud and plants out of low spots. The cleared hole fills with water. In the dry season, it can be some of the only water around.

Fish, turtles, snails, and birds crowd in. The alligator eats some of them, but many more survive until the rain comes back.
wow.insetCap: An alligator and its baby in the Everglades.

keyIdea: Everything in nature is connected. Weather shapes which plants grow. Plants shape which animals survive. Animals shape the soil and water. A change in one part causes a chain of changes through the rest. This is a system: a set of parts that depend on each other. People can harm any part of the system, and people can choose to protect it.

quiz.q: What does it mean when scientists say living things in an ecosystem are "interdependent"?

options.t: They live in the same climate but don't interact with each other.
options.miss: Think about a food web. When the plants in a pond die, what happens to the fish that eat them? Their lives are linked.

options.t: They depend on each other to survive. What happens to one affects the others.
options.ok: 🌎 Exactly! Interdependence means living things are connected. Pull on one thread and the whole web moves.

options.t: They compete for food but never work together.
options.miss: Think about a food web. When the plants in a pond die, what happens to the fish that eat them? Their lives are linked.

quiz.q: A long drought hits a Florida wetland, and water levels drop too low for fish to survive. What would most likely happen to the wading birds that eat those fish?

options.t: Nothing. Birds always find other food easily.
options.miss: If the fish that birds eat disappear, what would the birds have to do? Think about what you would do if your food ran out.

options.t: The birds would grow larger with less competition.
options.miss: If the fish that birds eat disappear, what would the birds have to do? Think about what you would do if your food ran out.

options.t: The birds would struggle to find food and might leave the area or decline.
options.ok: 🌿 Yes! When one part of a food web collapses, the living things that depend on it feel the effect. That's a chain reaction.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of humans having a positive impact on an ecosystem?

options.t: A conservation team restores water flow to a wetland cut off by a canal.
options.ok: ⭐ That's it! Restoring water flow gives the ecosystem what it needs to recover. That's human impact in a helpful direction.

options.t: A city builds a road through a forest to connect two neighborhoods.
options.miss: Think about what a healthy wetland needs: water, native plants, natural patterns. Which answer gives it those things back?

options.t: A factory dumps oily waste into a river.
options.miss: Think about what a healthy wetland needs: water, native plants, natural patterns. Which answer gives it those things back?
